title: Four ways I build a formation-forward classroom
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Paul Matthews argues that in an age of AI, education must prioritize student formation—who students are becoming—over task completion. When students desire only to complete assignments, AI misuse becomes a logical shortcut; but when they desire genuine formation, outsourcing their work becomes illogical because you cannot outsource becoming someone. Matthews describes four practices from his classroom as Head of HASS and Christian Studies at a Christian secondary school. First, he launches each year with an explicit formation vision shared with students, not just a course outline. Second, he integrates that vision into formal assessments, requiring students to reflect on how the work has changed them. Third, he deliberately uses formation language throughout lessons—"formation goal" instead of "learning goal" and framing every task as producing a person, not a document. Fourth, he uses the Survey/Way/Stay assessment-launch routine: five minutes surveying the task, five minutes planning the execution, and five minutes asking students what they want to stay with them as a result of the work—what they want to know and who they want to become.
points: When students are oriented toward formation rather than completion, AI misuse becomes illogical: you cannot outsource becoming someone
Four practices shift a classroom toward formation: explicit vision launch, integrating vision into assessments, using formation language, and the Survey/Way/Stay assessment routine
The Survey/Way/Stay routine begins every assessment by asking students what they want to carry forward—framing academic work as transformation rather than production
quotes: My sons have been staying with the in-laws for a few nights (we were pretty sure the baby was coming so sent them off as a preemptive strike).
With our new-found (but short-lived?) mobility, we managed to go and see the Odyssey - brilliant!
I’ve also rediscovered my love for instrumental progressive jazz.
Anyway - over the last few weeks we’ve been thinking about a formation-forward vision for education.
A quick look in the rearview AI misuse has a gravitational pull amongst our students.
Many of our students have an ever-burning yet unconsumed desire for the path of least resistance, and that path now leads through a chatbot.
While there’s been much said about how we adjust our tasks in light of the AI reality, I want to go deeper.
It’s fast, it’s frictionless, and it produces something that looks like work.
